P.n: National Museum of the U.S. Air Force
P.w: The marquee: world's largest and oldest military aviation museum, 4 hangars of aircraft from the Wright 1909 Military Flyer to an SR-71, XB-70 and presidential planes. Free admission, free parking, open daily 9-5.

65-acre Dayton History campus built around the original 1905 Wright Flyer III, the only airplane that is a National Historic Landmark, gifted by Orville Wright himself and shown in a purpose-built pit.
NPS-run bike shop where the Wright brothers designed and built the machines that led to the 1903 first flight; the anchor of Dayton Aviation Heritage NHP in the Wright-Dunbar district. Free.

The 84-acre pasture where the Wrights perfected controlled, powered flight in 1904-05 and ran the world's first flying school. NPS site on WPAFB, free, with an interpretive center at the Wright Memorial.

NPS visitor center in the Wrights' former print-shop building; tells the intertwined stories of Wilbur, Orville and their classmate, poet Paul Laurence Dunbar. Free, gateway to the Wright-Dunbar aviation trail.
Orville Wright's grand 1914 Oakwood mansion (a National Historic Landmark) where he lived until his death; toured by advance-reservation shuttle from Carillon Park on Wednesdays and Saturdays.
1930 Italian-Renaissance-villa art museum overlooking downtown, with 20,000+ works across 5,000 years; anchors the Grafton Hill bluff. Open Wed-Sun.
Reconstructed Fort Ancient (c. 1200 CE) Native American village and solar-calendar site on the Great Miami River, a National Historic Landmark now operated by Boonshoft; open seasonally.
Hands-on science-and-nature museum with a planetarium, small zoo and children's exhibits north of downtown; the region's top family science destination.
Downtown riverfront park at the Great Miami confluence: Five Rivers Fountain of Lights, splash pad, winter ice rink, kayak and bike rentals, and the hub of the region's paved trail network. Free.

Dayton's oldest neighborhood and nightlife heart: a quarter-mile of brick-lined East Fifth Street lined with bars, restaurants and shops, named an APA Great Street. Best-preserved 1820-1915 architecture in the city.
1904 Flemish-façade glass-domed arcade, a downtown landmark reborn after a $162M restoration wrapped in 2025 (Hilton Garden Inn, food hall, shops); the rotunda dome is the showpiece.

1841 garden cemetery and 200-acre arboretum on rolling hills; resting place of the Wright brothers, Paul Laurence Dunbar, Erma Bombeck and Charles Kettering, with a Tiffany-windowed Romanesque chapel. Free.
189-acre MetroPark of formal gardens, a butterfly house, edible-landscape and towering observation tower south of the city. Open daily, free.
17-foot pink-granite obelisk on Wright Brothers Hill (dedicated 1940 on Orville's birthday) with an overlook across Huffman Prairie and the Mad River valley. Free.
World's largest collection of Packard automobiles and memorabilia, displayed inside a beautifully restored original 1917 Packard dealership showroom downtown.

1850 Greek Revival courthouse modeled on the Temple of Hephaestus, on whose steps Lincoln gave an 1859 anti-slavery speech; now the Montgomery County Historical Society museum in Courthouse Square. Free.

P.n: Paul Laurence Dunbar House Historic Site
P.ad: 219 Paul Laurence Dunbar St, Dayton, OH 45402
P.w: 1904-06 home of pioneering Black poet Paul Laurence Dunbar, preserved with his belongings; Ohio's first state memorial to an African American (1936) and part of the aviation-heritage park.
1,000-acre preserve with 25 miles of trails, cascades and the iron-orange Yellow Spring that named the village; the day-trip centerpiece. $10 parking.
Dramatic dolomite-and-limestone gorge cut by the Little Miami River, a National Natural Landmark with cliff-edge trails; adjoins John Bryan State Park.
752-acre park called the most scenic in western Ohio, wrapping the Little Miami gorge with hiking, camping, rock climbing and a disc-golf course.
Paved rail-trail on a National Scenic River corridor; the Yellow Springs Station (old depot, restrooms, parking) is a favorite trailhead for an easy bike ride into the village and gorge.
National Audubon center with a working sustainable farm, prairies and woodland trails northwest of the city; a hands-on nature draw for families. Open Tue-Sun.
Downtown home of the Dayton Dragons, holders of pro sports' longest consecutive sellout streak (1,600+ games); a beloved summer-evening institution on Monument Avenue.
Five Rivers MetroParks' year-round public market in a restored railroad freight house downtown; 50+ local growers, makers and prepared-food vendors. Free admission and parking, open Fri-Sun.
One of the oldest continually operating theaters on the continent, opened 1866 as the Turner Opera House; a restored 1,154-seat National Register venue for Broadway tours, concerts and film.

P.n: Benjamin & Marian Schuster Performing Arts Center
P.w: Dayton's flagship performing-arts center (opened 2003), home to the Dayton Philharmonic, Opera and Ballet under a fiber-optic 'Wintergarden' star ceiling.
Riverfront MetroPark at the confluence of the Stillwater and Great Miami rivers, with a rowing boathouse, playground and a red bridge linking the Great Miami and Stillwater river trails.
Small riverside MetroPark at the confluence of the Mad and Great Miami rivers offering the best unobstructed view of the downtown Dayton skyline and RiverScape fountains.
437-acre MetroPark on the Mad River with a 185-acre lake for boating, sailing, fishing and paddling, plus ponds, trails and prime birdwatching.
Wooded Kettering MetroPark laid out with input from the Olmsted firm; ridge and valley hiking trails, stone shelters and the historic Dogwood Pond.

Intimate 4,300-seat outdoor amphitheater (opened 1991) in Kettering's Lincoln Park Civic Commons, named for pop-top inventor Ermal Fraze; a summer calendar of national concerts, comedy and free festivals.
Rolling MetroPark in Bellbrook famous for the Osage Orange Tunnel (an 1880s fence-row grown into an arching green corridor) and the Three Sisters, a trio of oaks dating to the 1440s.
1,900-acre MetroPark around the Stillwater River and Englewood dam, home to three waterfalls (Martindale, Patty and Oaks) reached along the 3.8-mile Green Trail.
88-acre MetroPark along the Stillwater River with formal English, Federal and Victorian gardens, a Children's Discovery Garden and woodland boardwalk.
West Dayton MetroPark with a working educational farm, fishing at Argonne Lake and trails through the former Argonne Forest amusement park grounds.
Ohio History Connection museum on the Wilberforce/Central State campuses documenting African American history and culture, from the Great Migration to civil-rights-era Ohio.
One of the largest water-powered grist mills still standing (built 1802) above the Little Miami gorge in Greene County; a working mill and restaurant, and host of a 4-million-light Christmas display.

Wright's only Prairie-style residence in Ohio (his first Ohio commission), designed 1906, built 1908, restored inch-by-inch in a $5.3M project reopened in 2005. On the National Register; hourly guided tours Tue-Sat 11-5, Sun 1-5. The marquee mid-corridor sight.

Depression-era folk-art masterpiece: unemployed molder Ben Hartman spent 1932-44 building a sprawling miniature world of hand-set stone and pebble monuments (Independence Hall, a castle, biblical and patriotic scenes) in his own yard. Preserved by the Kohler Foundation; free, open daily dawn-dusk. A nationally noted grassroots-art landmark.
The only Smithsonian Affiliate art museum in Ohio (affiliated since 2012). Regional collection strong on American art, plus rotating exhibitions, set at the edge of Cliff Park downtown.

The Clark County Historical Society's museum in Springfield's grand 1890 Romanesque former City Hall and Market House. Local history from the Ice Age through Springfield's industrial heyday (Rogers greeting cards, farm machinery), plus a cafe under the rotunda.

A Federal-style 1839 stagecoach tavern and inn built on the National Road, once a stopover for drovers and Conestoga-wagon pioneers. Saved from demolition by the DAR's Lagonda Chapter, run as a museum since 1941; on the National Register since 1973. Open limited days.

P.n: George Rogers Clark Park & Battle of Peckuwe Site
P.w: Riverside park on the site of the 1780 Battle of Peckuwe, the largest Revolutionary War engagement west of the Alleghenies, where Col. George Rogers Clark's forces met the Shawnee. Trails, monuments to Clark and Tecumseh, and the Davidson Interpretive Center (across Lower Valley Pike).

P.ad: W Main St at Fisher St (National Road Commons), Springfield, OH 45504
P.w: The first of twelve identical DAR pioneer-mother monuments placed along the National Old Trails Road from Maryland to California, dedicated July 4, 1928 (Harry Truman attended). Springfield's was the first dedicated; moved in 2011 to National Road Commons downtown.

Restored formal gardens, arboretum and a Kiwanis children's garden within historic Snyder Park along Buck Creek, run by the National Trail Parks & Recreation District. Free public gardens, a horticulture and pollinator showcase.

P.n: Buck Creek State Park / C.J. Brown Reservoir
P.w: 1,900-acre ODNR park on the 2,120-acre C.J. Brown Reservoir just northeast of Springfield: swimming beach, marina, campground, cabins and trails, and a birding hotspot. From I-70 take Exit 59 north on SR-41.

P.ad: Indian Dr at Mound Circle, Enon, OH 45323
P.w: Ohio's second-largest conical burial mound (after Miamisburg), about 40 ft high and 574 ft around, built by the Adena culture roughly 2,000 years ago and preserved on a residential circle in Enon. Owned by the village; free to view.

Greene County Parks preserve with ~6 miles of trails winding along the Little Miami National Scenic River, a 2.3-mile River Loop, a nature center, canoe/kayak launch, primitive camping and a raptor aviary. Free, open daily.

17-mile paved rail-trail linking Xenia Station to Eastwood MetroPark in Dayton, crossing over I-675; the Beavercreek Station trailhead has restrooms, parking and the city's 9/11 memorial. A backbone of the Miami Valley's 340-mile trail network. Free.

Former limestone quarry, now Fairborn's second-largest park, exposing two of the oldest Silurian fossil coral reefs in the U.S. — one of the largest, most diverse Silurian-fauna sites in the world. Self-guided fossil trail; keep what you find in the spoil piles. Free, open daily.

Quirky, walkable Main Street at the gates of Wright-Patterson: Foy's — five nostalgic stores including a 1929 Halloween & variety shop — the macabre Secret Chamber house of oddities, indie boutiques, and a big third-weekend-of-October Halloween Festival with a Spooktacular Parade.

The region's premier 11,200-seat arena (opened 1990) on the Wright State campus by Wright-Patterson: home of Raiders basketball and a regular tour stop for national touring concerts, comedians and family shows.

Family-owned, award-winning estate winery on 200 acres near the headwaters of Caesar Creek in Greene County; tasting room pours estate wines and cider with a vineyard view. A member of the Ohio Wine Producers Association.

Kettering's community arts hub since 1986: the 1,800-sq-ft Kettering Health (Rosewood) Gallery shows contemporary local, regional and national artists across four exhibitions a year, plus studios, classes and the signature Art on the Commons festival each August. Free.

P.ad: 2230 E Centerville Station Rd, Centerville, OH 45459
P.w: 194-acre natural area along 1.75 miles of Sugar Creek, named for the founder of the Centerville-Washington Park District; color-coded trails wind past meadow, forest, an apiary and the Five-Fingered Sycamore, with Ordovician fossils in the creek. The park's master plan won a state first-place conservation award. Free.

P.ad: 255 W Spring Valley Rd, Centerville, OH 45458
P.w: Centerville's 60-acre flagship park, anchored by the Community Amphitheater — reopened after a 2025 renovation — that hosts a free Sunday-evening summer concert series with grass-terrace seating, food trucks and a pondside deck. Also walking trails, disc golf and a Veterans Memorial Plaza.

187-acre Centerville-Washington nature park of creeks, meadow, prairie and wetland habitats; the Kennard Nature Nook hosts programs and the Mark Kreusch natural playground, with trails threading the whole preserve. Free.

Historic 1854 farmhouse, barn and gazebo on 15 acres in Kettering, tracing to a Revolutionary War veteran granted the land; run by Kettering Parks and used for weddings, programs and community gatherings — a preserved slice of early Montgomery County.

P.n: Rose Music Center at The Heights
P.w: 4,200-seat fully covered outdoor amphitheater in Huber Heights (opened 2015), the north suburbs' marquee live-music venue — a full season of national touring acts under a weatherproof shelter, with lawn, terrace and box seating.

Five Rivers MetroPark on the site of vanished canal town Tadmor: 8+ miles of trail with real elevation, old-growth forest and Great Miami River overlooks, remnants of the 1845 Miami-Erie Canal, and a stretch of the Buckeye and North Country national trails. Free.

The heart of Troy: a traffic-circle square with a lively fountain and gardens, ringed by Victorian storefronts, shops and restaurants — the whole square is on the National Register of Historic Places. The fountain runs red each June for the Strawberry Festival.

1914 Romanesque mansion bequeathed to the people of Troy by Mary Jane Hayner in 1942; now the town's cultural hub with year-round exhibits, concerts and classes. Admission-free, and most events are free too.

The funky, creative heart of the day trip: 75+ independent shops, galleries, pubs and eateries along Xenia Avenue — Dark Star Books, the Yellow Springs Toy Company, Village Artisans, the historic Little Art Theatre — plus Antioch College and the twice-yearly Street Fair (second Saturdays of June and October).

Big reservoir park spanning Warren, Clinton and Greene counties — Ohio's premier fossil-hunting site, with a permit-and-palm-size rule letting visitors keep Ordovician brachiopods and corals from the designated zone, plus a 1,200-ft swimming beach, boating and miles of trails.

F.w: The originator of Dayton-style pizza (est. 1965): a cracker-thin crust cut into small squares, sold by the million each year. This N. Dixie location is a longtime local flagship.
Dayton's beloved chocolatier since 1926; every piece is still made by hand at the Wayne Avenue factory built around Esther's own house. The caramel creams and assorted boxes are the classics.
A 24/7 Centerville institution since 1979, named to national 'best donut' lists (People, USA Today) and a perennial Best of Dayton winner. The airy glazed yeast donut is the one to get.

Cash-friendly Dayton supper club since 1947, no reservations, pine-paneled and unchanged; the NY Times called it one of the world's 10 greatest traditional dining rooms. Steaks come with the legendary stewed tomatoes.
Dayton's bourbon house since 1942: 800+ whiskeys, single-barrel pours and craft cocktails at an Edwardian hand-carved wood bar. Consistently rated among the nation's best whiskey bars.
Dayton's oldest continuously operating tavern, in an 1839 Oregon District building; a patio, live music and pub plates. The history is the draw as much as the beer.
Oregon District taproom (since 2011) with a rotating craft-beer list, pub fare and one of the city's most extensive vegan menus. Reliable pre- or post-show spot on Fifth.

F.ad: 903 E Dixie Dr, West Carrollton, OH 45449
F.w: Family-run (Castro family) West Carrollton mainstay of 45+ years serving Spanish and Latin American tapas, paella and a deep wine list; a Dayton special-occasion favorite.
Upscale-casual Oregon District kitchen of world-fusion cuisine with strong Peruvian roots — ceviche, lomo saltado — plus two patios and full bars looking onto Fifth Street.
Chef-owner Emily Mendenhall's Oregon District bistro (since 2013) with daily-changing seasonal menus blending American Southern and tropical flavors, plus a tiki-inspired cocktail program.
Longtime South-of-downtown bistro with a lush, eclectic dining room serving Mediterranean-leaning New American plates; a Dayton date-night standby.
The nation's only production brewery inside a museum: costumed brewers make beer to mid-19th-century Dayton recipes on replica equipment at Carillon Park, paired with historic immigrant fare.
Dayton's flagship craft brewery (since 2014) in a downtown former foundry; Best of Dayton brewery winner. Ermal's Cream Ale honors the local inventor of the pull-tab can.
Working dairy farm (Young family since 1869) just north of Yellow Springs: homemade ice cream, farmstead cheese, a petting barn, mini-golf and driving range — the classic day-trip stop.

Chef Elizabeth Wiley's Oregon District spot (since 2013) for creative deck-oven pizzas (the Bright Eyes with zucchini and lemon), pastas and eggplant fries, with plenty of gluten-free and vegetarian options.
Popular soul-food kitchen inside West Social Tap & Table in the historic Wright-Dunbar district: oxtails, fried chicken, candied yams, mac & cheese and collard greens.

F.ad: 3464 Pentagon Blvd Ste D, Beavercreek, OH 45431
F.w: The Dayton area's best-known and best-rated pho house — a family-owned Beavercreek kitchen keeping its broth close to the family's Vietnamese recipe. Google 4.7 across ~2,000 reviews; Dayton937's "Quest for the Best Pho" ranks it the region's top bowl.

An east-Dayton institution serving classic Vietnamese — pho, vermicelli plates, fresh bubble tea — for more than 30 years. Consistently top-rated (Google 4.5, RestaurantGuru 4.8 across 750+ reviews); Dayton937 calls it a family-run room where two visits make you a regular.

A Centerville institution since 1987 and a perennial "Best of Dayton" Best-Chinese winner — tiki-tinged dining room famous for its Cottage Chicken and rock-salt prawns, with 1,300+ reviews behind its reputation.

One of the Dayton area's best-regarded sushi rooms — Google 4.6, ranked #8 of 71 Centerville restaurants on Tripadvisor across 650+ reviews — and a rare local Korean kitchen, run by local owners, plating nigiri and maki alongside Korean mains.

A can't-miss Beavercreek hidden gem: the Dayton Daily News profiled this 'inconspicuous little pink building' as cranking out some of the best authentic Thai food in Dayton, singling out the tamarind-coated pad thai and the crunchy fried bananas. Family-run and generous with portions; Dayton Local (Gem City) lists it among the area's top Thai. Google/RestaurantGuru strong across 230+ reviews.

A family-owned Riverside room (near Wright-Patterson) serving authentic Vietnamese and Chinese since the 1980s — about 15 pho broths including vegetarian, plus banh mi and vermicelli. Named in Dayton937's 'Quest for the Best Pho' as one of the region's genuine pho stops ($10–12 for pho, roll and tea); regulars call it the best Vietnamese in Dayton, with 400+ reviews behind it.

F.ad: 2733 Fairfield Commons Unit A, Beavercreek, OH 45431
F.w: A distinctive Viet-Cajun mashup at Fairfield Commons (the former Flyby BBQ space): build-your-own Cajun seafood boils — crawfish, crab, shrimp, mussels with corn and potatoes — alongside a full Vietnamese menu of pho, grilled-pork vermicelli and pork-chop rice. Both the Dayton Daily News and Dayton937 covered the opening; one Vietnamese reviewer called its pho the best in Dayton.

A Taiwanese bubble-tea shop and Vietnamese deli — boba, bubble waffles, mochi donuts, Korean corn dogs and Vietnamese-style coffees and smoothies. The Dayton Daily News tracked the local mini-chain to its third location at The Greene in Beavercreek; popularity across its Riverside and Miamisburg shops carried it to the region's premier retail center.

Beavercreek's viral conveyor-belt sushi arrival (former Jason's Deli space): nigiri, sashimi and specialty rolls rotate past on a belt, with iPad ordering at each table. The Dayton Daily News covered its July soft opening and WDTN tracked the Cincinnati-born concept to Beavercreek; a CityBeat review praised the freshness and 'all around excellent' service. Google 4.5 out of the gate.

A specialist Chinese noodle house in Kettering built around southern-Chinese fish-noodle soup — bouncy rice noodles, fish, fried yellow peas on the side and a build-your-own spice level via pepper oils. Owners Yaqin Jing and Zeng Siong ran four restaurants in southern China before opening here; Dayton937 gave it a dedicated feature. Google 4.7 / RestaurantGuru 4.6 across 130+ reviews — a genuine hidden gem, not a generic buffet.

An upscale, metropolitan sushi-and-Asian room in Kettering with a bar and patio. The Dayton Daily News 'First Look' said it impresses and singled out impeccably fresh fish on rolls like the 5th Ave.; Dayton937's Jon Hung called it 'a gem you have to try.' Google 4.5 across 280–380 reviews — the area's higher-end sushi standout.

Chef Dane Shipp's second concept (after Culture in the Oregon District), inside The Silos food hall downtown: Asian-inspired hot and cold noodles, bao and dumplings rooted in the Lao home-cooking Shipp learned from former roommates — e.g. a chicken ramen finished with collards. WDTN's Living Dayton featured its signature menu and the Dayton Daily News covered it as The Silos' debut vendor; Cincinnati/Dayton creator CutieTheFoodie (~51.7K TikTok) filmed the ramen, bao and street corn on site.
Dayton's first craft brewery in over 50 years (est. 2012), anchoring the Oregon District with 32 rotating house taps plus whiskey, cocktails, live music and art shows.
Acclaimed artisan brewery and winery on Wayne Avenue known for mixed-fermentation and barrel-aged farmhouse ales; a beer-nerd destination just east of the Oregon District.
One of the nation's only co-op-owned brewpubs (3,000+ member-owners) in a St. Anne's Hill building serving food and drink since 1856; scratch pub fare a short walk from the Oregon District.

F.n: Little Fish Brewing Company - Dayton Station
F.w: The Athens-born brewery's Dayton Station in historic Webster Station; farmhouse ales, lagers and wood-fired pizzas in a restored early-1900s building.
Downtown microbrewery near RiverScape pouring hand-crafted flagship and seasonal beers with a full pub kitchen.
Centerville's canal-themed brewpub (est. 2013) pairing house beer with an elevated gastropub menu; the original Lock 27 location.
Kettering's brewpub and Dayton's only customer-brewing facility, with 18 house taps of award-winning ales and lagers, root beer and cold brew in a 20,000-sq-ft taproom.
Salem Avenue soul-food and BBQ spot serving ribs, smoked wings, fried catfish and classic soul sides.
Downtown Miamisburg institution since 1986 in a historic canal-town building, famous for People's-Choice award-winning ribs in its house Q Sauce.
Longtime Oregon District favorite for authentic Thai in a high-ceilinged former packing plant; curries, noodles and a sushi bar.
Family-run taqueria (est. 2005) widely called Dayton's most authentic Mexican, known for tacos al pastor, birria and menudo.
Third-wave coffee bar that helped launch Dayton's specialty scene and grew its own roasting arm, Wood Burl Coffee.
Funky downtown coffeehouse and wine bar in the Fire Blocks District, community-minded with a menu honoring Dayton legends.
Dayton's beloved small-batch coffee roaster since 1973 (second-generation family-run); the Vandalia roastery cafe is the flagship.
Family-owned Oregon District tavern and live-music venue (est. 2008) known for its half-pound burgers, fried pickles and pickle soup.
Old North Dayton institution since 1990 serving homemade German, Polish, Lithuanian and Hungarian dishes in a 1910 building.

Yellow Springs' destination restaurant and an Ohio farm-to-table pioneer — open since 1977, sourcing local before the term existed, with a seasonal menu that turns over every two months. Reviewed at length by Columbus Monthly (Jan 2025) as 'seasonal, locally sourced fare' and featured by Dayton937; reservations via Resy. The corridor's clearest sit-down gem, on the Greene County edge of the Springfield midpoint.

Widely called the best restaurant in Springfield — a New American fine-dining room (‘clean, powerful food,’ full bar, live piano) tucked on a downtown side street. The Springfield News-Sun lists it among the city's best; the Visit Greater Springfield CVB carries it as a featured dining destination. Measured: 4.3 across ~515 RestaurantGuru reviews. Dinner Tue–Sat.

A Springfield institution near Wittenberg since 1977, famous for its signature STEAMED sandwiches — meat, cheese and condiments softened together in a special steamer. The Dayton Daily News profiled the method ('Deli's history is a steamy story'); the Springfield News-Sun and the Visit Greater Springfield CVB both carry it. Closed briefly, reopened under Springfield locals Eric & Tracy Mader (per News-Sun); active with 2025–26 reviews and the upstairs Press Box bar back open.

An authentic English pub in the village of Enon (pop. ~3,000), opened April 2022 by Adrian & Maggie Shergill, who moved from England — shepherd's pie, fish & chips, bangers & mash and craft ale in a converted garage that opens onto a patio, plus a proper monthly high tea begun for the Platinum Jubilee. The Springfield News-Sun ran a full photo feature; Hub Springfield covered the opening. A genuine immigrant-owned gem the corridor maps miss.

The social heart of downtown Springfield since 2016, in a restored 100-year-old warehouse with a 9,000 sq ft beer garden. BeerAdvocate named it one of the 34 best new U.S. breweries of its opening year (out of 861); the respected beer magazine Pellicle ran a full feature, and the Springfield News-Sun covered the national recognition. Rotating food trucks and Burgers & Brews nights.

A log-cabin icon that started as a late-1940s drive-in (founded 1947) and has served Springfield ~79 years, best known for its pizza. The Springfield News-Sun counts it among Clark County food businesses 'with long roots in the community'; carried by the Ohio.org state tourism site and the Visit Greater Springfield CVB. Small, packed on weekends — a genuine local landmark.

F.ad: 25 S St Clair St, Dayton, OH 45402
F.w: Downtown handmade bakery (owner Paige Woodie) that went viral in 2024 after Ohio creator Emily Pentecost's reel declared it the best bakery in the state (~2.5M views); traffic jumped ~500% and it now regularly sells out by early afternoon. Known for flaky croissants and creative matcha/coffee drinks.

Fire Blocks District smash-burger spot (in the Jollity space) grinding a house beef blend butchered and aged on-site with bread baked daily; a TikTok favorite — Emily Pentecost called the smash burger and Thai chicken sando some of the best burgers she's had.

Oregon District chef-driven restaurant from Chef Dane Shipp serving 'elevated street food with a global influence' after years of pop-ups; an instant TikTok favorite (Emily Pentecost featured its bold, chef-driven menu).

Award-winning underground speakeasy hidden in the lower level of the Avant-Garde Building; its back room houses Dozo, a chef-driven omakase-style sushi 'permanent pop-up' (head chef Yudi Alviando). A viral social pick — Kait Lott's 'Don't Sleep on Dayton' hidden-bar video.
